idiom_name: aggregate.__iter__() returning an object with __next__() raising StopIteration
implementation_notes: Python bakes the GoF roles into the data model: the aggregate implements __iter__ returning an iterator object, the iterator implements __next__ (raising StopIteration at the end, and continuing to raise on every later call) plus __iter__ returning self, and for/in, comprehensions, unpacking and the builtins iter()/next() all dispatch on that protocol; collections.abc.Iterator/Iterable formalise the pair for isinstance checks and mixins. Write an explicit protocol class when the cursor state must be inspectable or the traversal needs operations beyond the protocol (peek, undo, position); otherwise a generator function or itertools is the shorter realization.
pitfalls: StopIteration must not escape a generator body: a bare next() or a return value triggers RuntimeError under PEP 479, so exhaustion has to be checked instead of relying on the exception.
Mutating a container while iterating it misbehaves: dicts/sets raise RuntimeError ('dictionary changed size during iteration') while lists silently skip or repeat elements.

Iterators are single-use; binding one to a name and looping twice yields nothing on the second pass - iterate the iterable (or call iter() again) rather than caching an iterator, and do not share one cursor across threads.

variants.name: Generator functions (yield / yield from)
variants.idiom_name: generator function with yield / yield from (generator object implements the protocol)
variants.implementation_notes: A generator function is the idiomatic way to implement the iterator protocol: calling it returns a generator object that already provides __iter__/__next__, each yield suspends the frame with its locals intact, and the code reads as a linear traversal; PEP 342 extends generators with send/throw/close and collections.abc.Generator documents the ABC. yield from (Python 3.3) delegates to a sub-iterable and flattens recursion without a manual loop, and itertools supplies the standard building blocks (chain/islice/groupby/tee). Prefer generators for new traversals; keep an explicit protocol class only when the cursor must expose more than next() or be serialisable with its state.
pitfalls: Generators are single-shot and silently so: a second for-loop over the same object produces nothing, so API signatures taking an iterator should say so and callers should pass the iterable.
The generator frame keeps references until exhaustion or close(), and abandoned generators hold resources; GeneratorExit/close() interactions with finally blocks are easy to get wrong.
Lazy generators hide when work happens: nothing runs until the first next(), exceptions surface at the consumer, and an unguarded infinite generator hangs a materialising call.
